items.title: Adwumawura Programme trains second cohort of young entrepreneurs in Bono East
items.description: Young entrepreneurs in the Bono East Region have completed the training phase of the second cohort of the government’s Adwumawura Programme, with beneficiaries exploring funding and market opportunities to grow their businesses. The programme, implemented under the National Entrepreneurship and Innovation Programme (NEIP), provides entrepreneurship training, startup support and mentorship to young Ghanaians seeking to establish or expand businesses. A Breakfast Meeting with Purpose AGRICo Hub, the region’s designated training service center for the programme, hosted a strategic Breakfast Meeting in Techiman to officially bring the Adwumawura Programme to a close. The event served as a crucial bridge between emerging entrepreneurs and local financial institutions, creating a platform for direct engagement and potential funding opportunities. The atmosphere was electric as young business owners—many of whom had spent the past five weeks immersed in intensive entrepreneurship and business development training—networked with representatives from banks and financial agencies, pitching their visions and exploring avenues for growth. What Beneficiaries Received The Adwumawura Programme offers a comprehensive support package designed to give young entrepreneurs a competitive edge: · Five weeks of intensive entrepreneurship and business development training · Access to grant support and startup equipment · Six months of structured post-training mentorship and coaching This holistic approach ensures that participants are not only trained but also adequately supported as they navigate the challenging terrain of business ownership. “A Programme That Delivers” Speaking at the Breakfast Meeting, Emmanuel Sarkodie, Manager of AGRICo Academy and In-Charge of the Digital Innovation Unit at AGRICo Hub, expressed confidence in the programme’s ability to transform lives. “This programme has what it takes to empower the participants to succeed in their own businesses,” he said. “In the long run, it will help create jobs for the unemployed in our community.” Emmanuel Sarkodie emphasised that the initiative goes beyond mere training—it is a catalyst for sustainable economic development in the region and beyond. Participants Speak: From Local Businesses to Global Markets The beneficiaries themselves were effusive in their praise for the programme, with many describing it as a turning point in their entrepreneurial journeys. One participant noted that the training had helped them “reposition themselves and their businesses by opening opportunities in the global market.” The sentiment was echoed by several others who expressed optimism about the future. “We have been empowered to partner with other agencies like the Association of Ghana Industries (AGI) and the Free Zones to help us export our products,” another participant shared. For these young entrepreneurs, the dream is not just personal success—it is about creating opportunities for others. Many expressed confidence that as their businesses expand, they will be able to “attract more hands,” thereby increasing their workforce and creating jobs for the masses. Targeting Ghana’s Youth The Adwumawura Programme specifically targets young Ghanaian citizens, typically aged 18 to 40, who have viable or existing businesses with the potential to scale. Applications for the 2026 second cohort opened around May 2026, with onboarding and intensive training kicking off in September. The programme aims to support youth-owned enterprises annually as part of broader government efforts to curb youth unemployment and drive local economic growth. A Model for Economic Transformation As Ghana continues to grapple with youth unemployment, initiatives like the Adwumawura Programme offer a glimmer of hope. By combining training, funding, mentorship, and market linkages, the programme is not just creating businesses—it is building a new generation of job creators. The Breakfast Meeting in Techiman was more than a closing ceremony; it was a statement of intent. These young entrepreneurs are ready to take on the world, and with the support of the Adwumawura Programme, they just might succeed.

items.title: Une indignation à deux vitesses (Par Souleymane Diam SY)
items.description: On nous a appris que la violence conjugale avait un sens unique : de l’homme vers la femme. C’est vrai, dans l’immense majorité des cas. Et il faut la combattre sans faiblesse. Mais à Sam Ndiaye, dans la commune de Fandène dans le département de Thiès, la violence a pris le sens inverse. Cheikhou Omar Ndiaye, quarante ans, a été mortellement poignardé dans son sommeil par son épouse. Alors qu’il poussait son dernier soupir, traîné jusqu’au seuil de sa concession en criant le nom de son bourreau, c’est tout un pan du tabou entourant les violences faites aux hommes qui volait en éclats. Le défunt cultivateur laisse derrière lui six enfants. Sa seconde épouse, présumée meurtrière, était enceinte au moment des faits. Et depuis, c’est le silence. Un silence assourdissant. Car si la victime avait été une femme poignardée par son mari à la suite d’une dispute, les réactions n’auraient pas tardé. Les communiqués d’indignation auraient afflué, les marches se seraient organisées, les plateaux de télévision auraient tourné en boucle.Mais parce qu’il s’agit d’un homme, l’émotion reste discrète, presque embarrassée. Ces deux poids, deux mesures interrogent la cohérence de nos discours sur les droits humains. Une vie humaine n’est-elle pas sacrée, quel que soit le sexe de celui qui la perd ? L’interdit d’ôter la vie ne doit souffrir ni exception ni lecture sélective. Au Sénégal comme ailleurs, des voix légitimes réclament l’inscription du féminicide dans le Code pénal, défini par les Nations Unies comme le meurtre d’une femme en raison de son genre, souvent sur fond de contrôle ou de possession. Pour conserver toute sa crédibilité morale, ce combat ne doit pas être à géométrie variable. Si l’on criminalise les meurtres liés au genre, la protection doit être absolue et bilatérale. Qu’en est-il alors des hommes victimes d’homicides ou de violences extrêmes au sein du couple ? Ce que l’on pourrait qualifier de « masculinicides », de l’affaire Aïda Mbacké au drame de Sam Ndiaye, prouve que la violence intrafamiliale n’est pas l’exclusivité d’un seul sexe. Dans notre société, la virilité reste associée à la stoïcité et au silence. Un homme ne doit ni pleurer, ni se plaindre, ni étaler ses faiblesses. Sous le poids de ces représentations, de nombreux époux souffrent dans une solitude absolue : maltraitance psychologique, violences physiques, chantage affectif, humiliations quotidiennes. Par peur de la risée du voisinage ou de l’incompréhension des proches, beaucoup se taisent et endurent jusqu’au drame ultime. D’autres, plus rares, tentent de briser l’isolement en cherchant du soutien auprès d’associations à l’image de celle des maris battus pour soulager un stress devenu insupportable. Cette initiative a contribué à élargir la définition de la violence conjugale au-delà des agressions physiques, en y intégrant ses manifestations psychologiques, morales, économiques et verbales. L’heure n’est pas à l’opposition entre les sexes, mais à la prise de conscience globale. La violence domestique, sous toutes ses formes, est un fléau. Revendiquer des lois plus sévères pour protéger les femmes est une cause noble et nécessaire. Mais occulter la souffrance d’hommes victimes de leurs conjointes affaiblit le principe même d’égalité devant la loi et devant l’empathie nationale. Il est urgent d’élargir le spectre de notre indignation, de briser le tabou du mari battu et de rappeler une vérité élémentaire : chaque vie supprimée par la violence conjugale est une tragédie de trop. souleymanediam.sy@lesoleil.sn

items.title: FIFA : quand Gianni Infantino loue des bureaux auprès de son ami Trump pour près de 4 millions de dollars
items.description: La Federation internationale de football association (FIFA) a conclu en mai 2025 un contrat de location de plus de sept ans pour des bureaux situes au 17e etage de la Trump Tower, a New York. Selon des documents internes consultes par Le Monde, l'instance s'est engagee a verser pres de 4 millions de dollars pour ces locaux de 450 metres carres, le plus souvent inoccupes. Le bail, entre en vigueur le 1er juin 2025, lie la filiale americaine de la FIFA, FIFA Americas Incorporation, a Trump Tower Commercial LLC, societe proprietaire et gestionnaire des lieux, presidee par Eric Trump, fils du president americain Donald Trump. Il a ete signe par quatre membres de la direction de la FIFA, dont son secretaire general Mattias Grafström. Le loyer represente en moyenne environ 470 000 dollars par an, soit quelque 41 000 dollars par mois. Ce montant augmente de 2 % chaque annee. La FIFA assure que ce loyer est conforme au marche et que le contrat respecte la legislation locale. Des interrogations sur les procedures internes Le choix de la Trump Tower suscite toutefois des questions au sein de l'organisation. Selon ces memes documents, la FIFA n'aurait pas visite d'autres locaux ni mis plusieurs offres en concurrence avant d'opter pour la Trump Tower. Des membres de son administration auraient egalement exprime des inquietudes au sujet d'un possible conflit d'interets et du respect des procedures habituelles. La commission des finances de la FIFA n'aurait, selon une source proche du dossier citee par le quotidien, ni ete informee de cette installation ni valide son coût. Les anciens et actuels responsables sollicites par Le Monde a ce sujet n'ont pas repondu. De son cote, la FIFA affirme que le bail a ete signe conformement a ses procedures internes. L'organisation justifie cette implantation new-yorkaise par la tenue de grands evenements sportifs, dont la Coupe du monde des clubs 2025 et la Coupe du monde 2026, organisee aux etats-Unis, au Canada et au Mexique. Elle indique que le bureau sert de point d'appui lors des deplacements de ses representants a New York et accueille des rencontres avec des dirigeants de federations, des responsables gouvernementaux et d'autres interlocuteurs. Le coût de ce bureau ne se limite pas au loyer. Une facture de pres de 100 000 dollars a ete adressee a la FIFA par la Trump Corporation en septembre 2025 pour des travaux de maintenance, d'electricite et de renovation. Des liens etroits entre Infantino et Trump Cette location s'inscrit dans un contexte de proximite affichee entre le president de la FIFA Gianni Infantino et Donald Trump. Infantino avait ete invite a la ceremonie d'investiture du dirigeant americain en janvier 2025. En decembre 2025, Infantino avait remis a Donald Trump le « Prix de la paix » cree par la FIFA lors du tirage au sort de la Coupe du monde 2026. Les initiatives du president americain dans certains dossiers lies au football ont aussi suscite des reactions, notamment lorsqu'il a plaide pour un allegement de la sanction visant l'attaquant americain Folarin Balogun. Les deux hommes s'etaient ensuite retrouves a la Trump Tower le 17 juillet 2026, deux jours avant la finale de la Coupe du monde, lors d'une reception organisee par la FIFA. Le bail court jusqu'a fin 2032, soit bien au-dela de la Coupe du monde 2026. La FIFA ne peut le resilier qu'a l'issue de cinq ans et sept mois, avec un preavis de 12 mois et le paiement d'une indemnite equivalant a six mois de loyer. Ces revelations surviennent alors que Gianni Infantino, a la tete de la FIFA depuis 2016, est candidat a un troisieme mandat lors de l'election prevue le 18 mars 2027. elu pour succeder a Sepp Blatter, il avait d'abord acheve le mandat de ce dernier, avant d'etre reelu en 2019 et en 2023.

items.title: In memoria : Ouédraogo Rufine Marie Clémence née Zaongo
Destroying Jimi River for gold could cost us our lives – Asantehene
items.description: Asantehene Otumfuo Osei Tutu II has warned that illegal mining driven by unemployment could cost communities their lives if rivers like the Jimi are destroyed. Speaking after inspecting the heavily degraded Jimi River and the Jimi Dam near Obuasi, the Asantehene said he understands why many young people turn to galamsey, but cautioned that irresponsible mining will leave lasting consequences. “I understand illegal mining has become an option because many young people have no jobs. But we cannot continue to do that because the river is also relevant to our lives. If we destroy the river, what happens to us then? We will give birth to deformed babies,” Otumfuo said. The Asantehene was visibly distraught after seeing how illegal miners at Tasliman had diverted the course of the Jimi River with heaps of sand, causing siltation and threatening the Jimi Dam which treats water for over 200,000 people in Obuasi and Adansi. He was accosted by some youth at the dam during the inspection, which is part of the 153-hectare Jimi Land Reclamation and River Watercourse Rehabilitation Project, a pilot under the Green Ashanti Initiative which is being led by Oheneba Nana Kwaku Dua with support from AngloGold Ashanti. “I understand unemployment is a challenge, but we must also think about the damage we are doing to the river. We may get the money, but we will die after the environment is destroyed. I know that if there is no employment, the youth will always go and mine. But we should also know that the river cannot be destroyed,” he stressed. The King called for a balance between job creation and environmental protection, urging responsible mining practices. “We can find ways of mining responsibly. Because of gold, many are also felling their cocoa farms. We may end up destroying ourselves and the environment. I will plead with you, if you turn to galamsey due to unemployment, it must be done responsibly, without destroying the environment,” he appealed. Otumfuo said he will take the matter before his chiefs to deliberate on lasting solutions. The Jimi reclamation project is expected to restore degraded lands in six steps and provide alternative livelihoods through kenaf and other tree farming. Two Ministers, the Lands and Natural Resources Minister, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah and Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs Minister, Mahama Ayariga, joined the Asantehene on the tour, which started with briefings at AngloGold Ashanti and tree planting at Lot 1 of the project.

items.title: Burkina: découvrez les innovations majeures sur la relecture de la loi portant travail d’intérêt général
items.description: Dans cet élément tiré du texte du ministère de la Justice, nous vous faisons découvrir les innovations majeures sur la relecture de la loi portant Travail d'intérêt général (TIG) qui a été validée le mercredi 14 octobre 2026 par les députés lors séance plénière à l’Assemblée nationale. Au titre des travaux éligibles à la peine de travail d'intérêt général (TIG) La relecture de la loi portant travail d'intérêt général consacre une innovation importante à travers la prise en compte des prestations intellectuelles parmi les travaux éligibles à cette peine. Au titre des infractions exclues du prononcé de la peine de travail d'intérêt général (TIG) La relecture de la loi prévoit l'exclusion explicite des infractions criminelles et de celles en lien avec le terrorisme du champ d'application de la peine de travail d'intérêt général. Au titre des conditions de commutation des peines d’emprisonnement en peine de travail d'intérêt général (TIG) L'une des innovations majeures réside dans l'introduction d'un régime permanent de commutation des peines d’emprisonnement en peine de travail d'intérêt général, en remplacement du régime transitoire précédemment en vigueur. Au titre des acteurs intervenant dans le travail d'intérêt général (TIG) La relecture de la loi consacre l'intervention de l'Administration pénitentiaire parmi les acteurs impliqués dans la mise en œuvre du travail d'intérêt général. Au titre du prononcé de la peine de travail d'intérêt général L’une des principales innovations envisagées est le prononcé d’office de cette peine pour certaines infractions mineures, conformément aux conditions prévues par la loi. DCRP-MJ L’article Burkina: découvrez les innovations majeures sur la relecture de la loi portant travail d'intérêt général est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: India voter purge
items.description: THE purge of millions of voters from India’s electoral rolls has sparked widespread demonstrations , spearheaded by young protesters calling for justice. The Cockroach Janta Party is at the forefront of the movement, while more established opposition parties, such as Congress, are also participating actively. The thread uniting these groups is their suspicion that the Indian election commission has been tinkering with the rolls to benefit the ruling BJP. Earlier this year, the youth-led CJP organised a massive anti-government campaign calling for the resignation of the education minister over exam irregularities. The movement succeeded in ousting the minister, with the youthful energy of its participants catching the BJP government off guard. This time too, India’s rulers have responded with brute force, bundling away thousands of protesters, including Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders, and cutting off access to the iconic Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi. Around 130m names have been removed from the electoral rolls. The Indian election authorities say the deleted names include voters who have died, relocated, or could not be traced. But the Indian opposition has dismissed this explanation. It is believed that many of the deleted voters were Muslims, as well as those belonging to other marginalised groups. Moreover, media reports say that the Indian election commissioner — whose resignation is being demanded — ignored objections from within the commission to the deletion of such a large number of voters. Such purging of the rolls is in keeping with the BJP regime’s marginalisation of vulnerable groups. It has employed lawfare and dubious means in the past as well to delete Muslim votes; millions have been disenfranchised through the National Register of Citizens. Earlier, the BJP and its Hindutva cohorts could get away with trampling the rights of Indian Muslims. But now, their shenanigans are not working. It appears that India’s other communities are also tired of Hindutva’s empty promises and its attempt to remake India in its own image through fair means and foul. The Sangh Parivar has run out of ideas, and its fantasies about a glorious Hindu past will not buy the people bread, or give them jobs. Hopefully, a fairer order can emerge from the tumult, in which all of India’s communities are treated equally. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

items.title: TTAP says 'no talks' with govt until meeting with Imran Khan is arranged, health details are provided
items.description: The Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) on Thursday announced that it was suspending all negotiations with the government, saying there would be “no talks” until a meeting with PTI founder Imran Khan was arranged and information about his health was provided. The alliance, in a statement, said all negotiating authority would rest solely with its chairman, Mehmood Khan Achakzai. The announcement was made at a leadership meeting held at Achakzai’s residence, where the political situation arising from the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in KP, as well as the situation in the province, was reviewed in detail. In the days preceding the development, political tensions between the federal government and the opposition, mainly the PTI, had remained high after the party announced a long march to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. However, the march, initially planned for Islamabad, remained confined to KP until it fizzled out with the imposition of governor’s rule in the province. The alliance strongly condemned the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in KP, describing the move as a “robbery” and a midnight assault on the Constitution and the people’s mandate. It demanded that the decision be withdrawn immediately, saying the step was not only an insult to the people of one province but to those of all provinces. The statement added that the alliance would also file a petition against the decision in the Peshawar High Court (PHC). The TTAP also condemned all forms of terrorism, including state terrorism against the public, actions by state institutions against political parties, and violence by one sect against another. Expressing full support for the National Action Plan, the opposition alliance demanded that, instead of adopting new policies, the joint resolution of the Aman Jirga approved by the KP Assembly be implemented immediately. The participants also demanded the immediate release of non-functional Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati, PTI provincial president Junaid Akbar, and all arrested members of the National and provincial assemblies and other leaders. The PTI had reported their detention on Oct 11, shortly after the Centre imposed emergency and governor’s rule in the province. The alliance also demanded the release of Imran Khan’s sisters, who have been in detention for nearly three weeks under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) Ordinance, as well as a meeting with the PTI founder and access to his doctors. The TTAP attributed the deteriorating law and order situation in Balochistan to the unrepresentative provincial government and the federal government’s failed policies, saying the provincial government had not been formed on the basis of the people’s genuine mandate. It called for the province’s issues to be resolved through dialogue with its people rather than the use of force. The alliance also announced plans to approach international human rights organisations and the United Nations over what it described as restrictions on judicial independence, media curbs and violations of human rights and the Constitution. Emergency over terrorism concerns On Sunday, the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and governor’s rule under Article 234. The decision came during a meeting of the federal cabinet, which deliberated on the security situation in PTI-led KP and noted the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. Subsequently, the prime minister sent a summary to the president, who approved the move. Soon after, the Centre also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. Meanwhile, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre sought to explain that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. On Monday, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar defended the governor’s rule, saying it was not politically motivated but instead taken to curb terrorism. The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks . The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban.

items.title: Révolte des lycéens en France: le signe du désarroi d’une jeunesse face à un système mondial à bout de souffle
items.description: Ceci est une tribune du Dr. Nurudine OYEWOLE, Expert-consultant en Communication, Expert en coopération transfrontalière et Analyste politique. Dans son document, il revient sur la crise qui secoue actuellement la France, notamment la révolte des lycéens. Pour lui, cela est « le signe du désarroi d’une jeunesse face à un système mondial à bout de souffle ». « Depuis le 18 septembre 2026, les lycéens français sont en colère contre le gouvernement et le président français Emmanuel MACRON. Partie depuis les territoires d’outre-mer, notamment à Cayenne en Guyane plus précisément au Lycée Félix Éboué, la révolte des lycéens français s’est propagée en Hexagone et depuis lors, ne baisse pas d’intensité. Au cœur des revendications lycéennes, il y a d’abord, les conditions d’études difficiles avec des classes vétustes, délabrées et insalubres ; le manque de tables-bancs, de chauffage en hiver et de moyens de ventilation pendant la canicule, etc. Ensuite, on dénombre des problèmes académiques, liés au manque de professeurs, aux emplois du temps surchargés et inadaptés, etc. Enfin, il y a des questions structurelles, notamment l’outil d’orientation Parcoursup, accusé de rejeter les élèves ayant eu le Bac et venant de quartiers difficiles ou du moins de les orienter vers des filières moins valorisantes. Cette révolte des lycéens, comme un feu de brousse, est en train de gagner d’autres secteurs. En effet, les étudiants ont rejoint la contestation et les gilets jaunes comptent leur apporter leur soutien en organisant des marches et meetings de soutien, face à un pouvoir qui semble dans l’incapacité d’apporter des réponses courageuses et concrètes aux manifestants. Dans la réalité, cette mobilisation exceptionnelle de la jeunesse française est l’expression de son désarroi et d’une bonne partie des Français face à un avenir incertain, avec une économie en berne et une société en manque d’imagination face à la bascule actuelle du monde. En effet, ne nous y trompons pas, la France et de nombreux pays occidentaux, traversent une crise profonde à trois niveaux. En premier lieu, cette crise est d’abord économique. Le modèle capitaliste et ultra-libérale qui marchandise toutes les transactions et interactions humaines, est à bout de souffle. Car, les principes mis en place pour le gouverner et l’entretenir se heurtent à la montée de nouvelles puissances qui mettent à mal ce système mondial impérial au profit de l’Occident. C’était valable et tenable quand l’Occident concentrait le cœur des activités commerciales et industrielles mondiales. Aujourd’hui, le centre de gravité de l’activité économique mondiale s’est déplacé en Orient avec la montée de la Chine. L’Occident est face à la nécessité de se réinventer pour ne pas disparaitre. D’où, la méthode à la Trump qui veut imposer son diktat par la force à travers des guerres et des surtaxes douanières. En deuxième lieu, cette crise est sociétale. En effet, le capitalisme et l’ultralibéralisme régnants ont consacré l’individualisme comme étant le moyen absolu de réaliser le bonheur de l’individu. L’individu étant dorénavant libre de ses choix au mépris de tout bonheur dans un cadre communautaire et collectif. Les structures mises en place par les États devant suppléer la communauté pour rendre ce bonheur effectif. Or, lorsque les crises perdurent et que l’État n’a plus de ressources pour faire face à ses obligations vis-à-vis de ses citoyens, l’individu n’a plus de recours, voire de filet de sauvetage en tant que tel. Il est obligé d’avoir paradoxalement recours à des communautés caritatives organisées (ONGs, associatives religieuses, fondations, etc.), voire son cercle familial. En troisième lieu, cette crise est écologique. En effet, le modèle de production du capitalisme et de l’ultralibéralisme régnants exploite les ressources naturelles comme si celles-ci sont inépuisables. Voilà qu’il aujourd’hui est confronté à la réalité de la finitude de ces ressources. Pourtant, malgré les alertes incessantes, des puissances mondiales, notamment les États-Unis sous Donald Trump refusent l’évidence et continuent une exploitation à outrance des ressources naturelles non renouvelables. À tout cela, s’ajoute l’Intelligence artificielle dont l’usage va bouleverser profondément la vie à tous les niveaux, avec des conséquences non encore prévisibles. En clair, le monde est à un point de bascule qui suscite beaucoup d’incertitudes. Le désarroi de la jeunesse française est aussi celui de la jeunesse mondiale. Il ne sera pas étonnant que cette révolte se propage dans de nombreuses parties du monde, avec une GEN’Z qui veut prendre son destin en mains face à la vieille garde qui refuse d’écouter ses inquiétudes, de se réformer et d’entamer les réformes nécessaires. » Dr. Nurudine OYEWOLE Expert-consultant en Communication Expert en coopération transfrontalière. Analyste politique L’article Révolte des lycéens en France: le signe du désarroi d’une jeunesse face à un système mondial à bout de souffle est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Pakistan worst hit by hunger in South Asia
items.description: • Economic instability erodes household purchasing power; heavy rains, floods trigger acute crop losses • ​South Asia remains in the ‘serious’ category; ​global hunger rises after two decades ISLAMABAD: Pakistan recorded the highest score in South Asia on the 2026 Global Hunger Index released on Wednesday, reflecting a worsening food security crisis driven by economic instability, climate shocks and global conflicts. Published jointly by Welthungerhilfe, the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict at Ruhr University Bochum, and the Swiss organisation Helvetas under the theme “No Security Without Food Security”, the report reveals that progress in South Asia has largely stagnated, with conditions in Pakistan and Afghanistan deteriorating since 2018. In Pakistan, economic instability and sharp food price inflation have eroded households’ purchasing power and constrained access to food. Undernourishment in the country has climbed from low in 2018 to medium, while child wasting has risen toward the high threshold. Across South Asia, the situation remains serious with a regional score of 23.5. Although the region’s score has fallen substantially from an alarming 37.5 in 2000, most of that progress occurred before 2018. While Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved from the alarming to the serious category since 2000, child stunting remains very high. Pakistan’s stunting rate continues to fall, whereas Afghanistan’s has edged up since 2018. Child mortality rates in both nations have declined from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels today. The report warned that high levels of acute food insecurity will persist across the region. Heavy rains and flooding caused localised crop losses in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh, while below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures negatively affected Afghanistan’s 2026 cereal-growing season. According to Food and Agriculture Organisation estimates, 218 million people in South Asia, including Iran, were undernourished between 2023 and 2025, representing roughly one-third of the global total. Globally, hunger is rising again after nearly two decades of progress. The 2026 global score stands at 18.1, worsening from 17.6 in 2018. Hunger has increased in 32 countries since 2018, and 57 countries are on track to miss achieving even low hunger levels by 2030. Three of the index’s four indicators — undernourishment, child stunting and child wasting — have worsened, while only child mortality has continued to decline slightly. State-based armed conflicts, now at their highest level since World War II, alongside frequent extreme weather events, are major drivers of this reversal. The war in Iran and shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait are driving up fuel, transportation and fertiliser costs. Meanwhile, Russia’s war in Ukraine and Black Sea export restrictions threaten higher wheat prices, making basic supplies unaffordable in the Global South. Compounding the crisis, international spending on food security has fallen to 2016-2017 levels, forcing cuts to aid programmes and emergency rations. The report urged governments to reverse funding cuts for humanitarian assistance and data collection to prevent and manage future crises. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

items.title: India expected to overtake Japan as world's 4th largest economy in 2027: IMF
items.description: India is expected to become the world’s fourth-largest economy by 2027, overtaking Japan, according to International Monetary Fund (IMF) projections that on Thursday laid out the Asian nations’ contrasting trajectories. The IMF said Japan would remain the fourth-largest country by nominal gross domestic product this year, but in 2027 India is set to take its place, with a GDP reaching $4.52 trillion. Japan is slated to slip to sixth place that year, falling behind both India and the United Kingdom, the projection showed. India has shown strong growth in recent years despite global economic headwinds, with the IMF this week raising its forecasts for 2026 growth to hit 7.0 per cent. Japan, by contrast, is plagued by an aging population and other structural problems that have seen the Asian giant’s growth stagnate. The United States is the world’s largest economy, followed by China and Germany. Releasing the IMF’s regional economic outlook for Asia-Pacific on Thursday, Asia Director Krishna Srinivasan said India entered the current energy price shock caused by the US-Israel war on Iran from a strong position. “India entered this with very strong fundamentals,” he said. “Growth was strong, fiscal prudence was pretty much enshrined, they had lots of reserves and so on. And so in that context, they have responded well to the shock.” Growth in Japan, by contrast, is projected to slow to 0.7pc in 2026, with the country hard hit by an increase in energy prices —and wider inflation— that has seen the Bank of Japan raise interest rates to their highest level in three decades. The country, long haunted by deflation, has seen a sustained increase in consumer prices since the spring of 2022, and spiking energy prices from the Iran war have further fuelled those rises. The fall of the yen, which hit its lowest level in 40 years against the dollar over the summer, is further driving up the cost of imports. Japan’s aging population is also weighing on economic activity. The IMF’s Srinivasan said Japan’s economy was benefiting from the boom in artificial intelligence investments, but not as much as its regional neighbours. The benchmark Nikkei index in Tokyo fell by nearly five percent on Thursday, dragged down by a plunge in tech stocks amid doubts over the profitability of the AI sector.

items.title: School collapses in Pakistan: A timeline of incidents since 2021
items.description: The roof of a private school in Peshawar’s Afridi Abad collapsed on Thursday, killing 33. The deceased included 32 students — between the ages of seven and 14 — and a female teacher. Pakistan has witnessed several incidents of structural collapses at educational institutions in recent years, resulting in the deaths and injuries of students, teachers and other staff members. Here is a timeline of reported incidents over the past five years. Sep 11, 2026 — Karachi, Sindh Five people were killed and two others injured when a wall of a dilapidated government school building collapsed on them in Orangi Town’s Sector 11. The school was closed at the time of the incident. July 2, 2026 — Lahore, Punjab A child died and at least five others were injured after the roof of an under-construction private school building collapsed in the Baghbanpura neighbourhood . The school administration was constructing a two-marla structure to expand its existing 14-marla building. The roof collapsed during the construction work, sending debris onto the boy and others, including a motorcyclist and several labourers. June 30, 2026 — Lahore, Punjab In Lahore’s Kahna area, 14 children were killed while several others were injured when the roof of a private tuition centre collapsed. A statement by the Edhi rescue service, which took part in the rescue operation, said that the roof “collapsed suddenly”. Lahore District Education Authority Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Tariq Mahmood said the building housed a private tuition centre and was run by a woman resident of the area. June 30, 2026 — Umerkot, Sindh Three girls, aged 3 to 13, were killed after a portion of the outer wall of a government primary school near Umerkot collapsed and the rubble fell on them. The girls were returning home after attending a nearby seminary. While they were passing by the wall, it suddenly collapsed, locals said, adding that the girls died before they could be rescued from under the rubble. May 7, 2026 — Dera Ghazi Khan, Punjab At least four children were killed and 20 people were injured after the roof of a classroom at a private school collapsed. The injured included 16 students, two teachers and as many labourers. A probe into the incident revealed that construction for an extension of the building was underway when the roof of the classroom collapsed. February 2026 — Sialkot, Punjab A student of Government Girls Higher Secondary School Bediana in Sialkot district was buried under the rubble of an under-construction structure that collapsed on her. The authorities registered a case against District Education Authority Chief Executive Officer Mujahid Hussain, school principal Kalsoom and the contractor following the incident. June 30, 2025 — Multan, Punjab Several girls were injured when the roof of a madressah collapsed. Rescue personnel pulled the girls trapped beneath the rubble out. Four girls were treated at the site, while five others received first aid before being shifted to Nishtar Hospital. Sep 26, 2024 — Muzaffargarh, Punjab A student died while six of his class fellows were critically injured when the roof of a private school collapsed in Wesandywali village . The incident happened at the Aligarh Public School. The owner had started the construction of a room on the upper floor without seeking permission. The ceiling of the old classroom could not bear the weight and collapsed. Aug 30, 2024 — Khairpur, Sindh Twelve students suffered head injuries when a large chunk of concrete plaster fell from the ceiling of a government high school classroom in Basiro village , Khairpur district. A viral video showed large, brick-sized chunks of concrete scattered across classroom desks, while students with bloodied heads and faces were being rescued and taken to hospitals. July 2, 2024 —Swat, KP Six children were injured when the roof of a classroom collapsed in Tangaar village , in Gwalerai Union Council of Swat’s Matta tehsil. The incident occurred in a nursery classroom at a private school. One of the walls collapsed before the roof caved in. May 9, 2024 — Layyah, Punjab Eight children were injured when the roof of their classroom collapsed at a private school in Chak 344/TDA, in Chaubara tehsil of Layyah district. The children were attending a pre-school class at Al-Rahman Grammar School when the roof collapsed on them. Feb 21, 2024 — Jacobabad, Sindh Four young students were injured when plaster fell from the ceiling of their classroom at the main government primary school for boys in Jacobabad . Teachers at the school said that plaster had fallen from the ceiling of a Grade Three classroom. The school building was in a dilapidated condition. July 4, 2023 — Okara, Punjab The roofs of three rooms and a portion of the veranda at the Government Elementary School collapsed just days before Eidul Azha, during summer vacation. The village school catered to 900 students. The affected area consisted of three rooms and a veranda used by the middle section students, totaling 300 in number. June 27, 2023 — Bannu, KP Three seminary students were killed and two others injured when a room’s roof collapsed in Bannu . The roof caved in when some workers were busy spreading clay over it to prevent leaks during rains. An official said many parts of the district had received heavy rain the previous night, and the roof of the seminary collapsed due to absorption of rainwater. Aug 26, 2022 — Muzaffargarh, Punjab At least 14 students were injured, 12 of them seriously, when the roof of a classroom collapsed in a private school in the Jinnah Garden locality. At the affected school, 65 students were studying from nursery to 5th grade. Oct 22, 2021 — Jhelum, Punjab Two students were killed and 20 other people — 16 students and four teachers — were injured when the wall of a school collapsed during an event inside the school situated along the GT Road in Jhelum . The students who died were both aged 15. June 7, 2021 — Lahore, Punjab A schoolboy was killed and three others were injured when the boundary wall of a private school collapsed on College Road in the Green Town area. A police official said the children were playing near the wall when it collapsed. Four of them were trapped under the debris. One died on the spot, while the other three suffered injuries. items.title: The Cards Ukraine Has Left to Play
items.description: U krainians have gotten used to awful news. But even by their standards, the past several days have felt dismal. Russian missile strikes are pounding Ukrainian cities relentlessly. Donald Trump announced a deal last week to buy Russian diesel fuel. Then came reports about disruptions in U.S. support to Ukraine, including the Starlink communication system. Together, these developments have caused alarm in Kyiv on a scale rarely seen since the start of the war. The only letup in the gloom appeared on Friday, when Ukrainians had a chance to imagine their tormentor, Vladimir Putin, aboard his presidential plane, seething as it circled over Moscow, unable to land in his own capital. A swarm of Ukrainian drones had forced the closure of the city’s airports that day—all four of them—as Putin flew home from a trip to Turkmenistan. His plane, known as the Flying Kremlin, does not appear to have been the target. “It was purely coincidental,” a military officer familiar with the operation told me. “Just a matter of chance.” Still, to many Ukrainians, it tasted briefly of revenge, and it showed that their military still has ways to hurt Russia’s economy and its leader, even if Trump decides to abandon them. On Tuesday night, nearly 500 drones attacked Moscow, again prompting the closure of its airports, according to the city’s mayor. Such methods may not be enough to force Putin to negotiate. But they allow Ukraine, if it chooses, to stay in the fight and keep up the pressure on Moscow to come to the table. Since early last month, Ukrainian drones have interfered with air traffic over the Russian capital almost every day, a version of a military operation code-named M&Ms, which The Atlantic first reported in August. The operation does not rely on U.S. technology or intelligence, two of its architects told me. Instead, it uses drones produced in Ukraine and equipped with AI guidance systems to bring the war to Russia. (Both sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military plans.) Such homegrown innovations could give Ukraine leverage in any future peace talks. But they do not bode well for the global state of aviation safety. Not since the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, have airports and airplanes looked more vulnerable. The Houthi rebel group, which is backed by Iran, launched two salvos of missiles and drones this weekend at the main airport in Riyadh, killing more than a dozen people and wounding hundreds. A week earlier, the U.S. Air Force evacuated a dozen bombers from an air base in England, reportedly due to a threat from Iranian drones. The spread of these weapons has made such attacks far cheaper and easier to stage. In early August, German authorities discovered a suspected Russian drone at an airport near Leipzig, apparently armed with explosives and prepared to blow up a Ukrainian cargo jet. A month later, Russian drones targeted Zelensky’s plane as it took off from Moldova on the way to Norway. “That is the reality he lives in,” Norway’s prime minister, who first reported the apparent attempt on Zelensky’s life, said. [ Read: Trump’s October surprise ] Many world leaders now live in that reality, even Putin. On the day of his diverted flight to Moscow, the Russian leader spent 90 minutes on the phone with Trump, who announced after their call that the United States would buy millions of barrels of Russian diesel. To protect that deal, Trump urged Ukraine to stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelensky has reluctantly complied in recent days. But his military has intensified attacks on other sensitive targets, which could prove no less disruptive for Russia’s economy and the lives of its people. The spate of attacks on Russian data centers in the past week has made that clear. S ince October 8 , Ukraine has bombed at least four Russian data centers, a class of targets it previously avoided. The attacks caused widespread outages of online services, including some of Russia’s most popular banking, delivery, map, and taxi apps. At Moscow’s airports, Ukrainian drones forced authorities to cancel 345 flights last week alone, according to a tally kept by Echo of Moscow , a Russian news outlet. “The Russian sky is becoming extremely dangerous,” Zelensky said on September 1, when he announced the start of the campaign to disrupt air traffic in Russia. “Civilian aviation has no place amid drones.” The two architects of this campaign told me that it is only just getting started. So far, Ukraine has used long-range drones to clog the airspace around Russian airports without striking them directly. In one incident this weekend, debris from a downed Ukrainian drone reportedly fell on the airport in Sochi, causing a fire at an administrative building. Zelensky has not yet allowed his military to proceed with the original plan for operation M&Ms, which called for much more aggressive tactics. According to the authors of the plan, the more ambitious version would use AI-guided drones to circumvent Russian air defenses and hit airports in Moscow and other cities. These drones will soon be manufactured at scale, one of the authors of the plan told me. Although Trump has intervened to secure supplies of Russian diesel, he has said nothing about the recent attacks on Russian airports and data centers. On the contrary, when he first called on Zelensky last month to stop bombing Russian oil refineries, he tempered his demand with an invitation for Ukraine to bomb something else. “There are plenty of other targets,” Trump said. [ Read: Trump’s latest appeal to Russia could outrage even his allies ] But the same holds true of Ukraine. Last month, when Zelensky began the M&Ms operation, Russia intensified its bombing of civilians, launching regular daytime strikes against apartment blocks, schools, and academic institutions. Such attacks serve no military purpose other than to terrorize the population. The most recent casualty report from the United Nations said that the Russian bombing campaign reached “a new level of intensity” last month, killing at least 200 civilians and injuring 1,234 from September 1 to 24, when the report came out. At this stage in the war, the escalations cut both ways. No matter what new weapons and tactics Ukraine deploys, Russia can always answer with more brutality. Trump no longer seems interested in stopping that cycle of violence. He has shifted from the role of mediator between warring sides to a dealmaker with the Russians, and that presents Zelensky with a stark choice: accept Trump’s and Putin’s demands to end the war on Russia’s terms or find new ways to continue fighting, with or without American support. A t the start of this year , when Ukrainian officials first offered Zelensky the M&Ms plan, he deemed it too dangerous. It called for as many as 1,000 drones to attack Moscow’s airports every day, making it impossible for civilian flights to operate. Zelensky allowed his defense minister at the time, Mykhailo Fedorov, to continue developing the AI-enabled drones required for the operation. But Zelensky kept a tight rein on their deployment, insisting that Fedorov minimize the risk to travelers, the two designers of the plan told me. My first report about the operation, published on August 20, led to an intense public debate about its morality. Many in Ukraine and allied Western countries noted that Russia has shown no qualms about bombing the innocent. “It’s not fair for one side to break all the rules of war while the other side holds back,” a senior European official told me of Zelensky’s hesitation. One of the architects of the plan told me that public pressure contributed to Zelensky’s decision to announce the start of the campaign on September 1. In a video address released that day, he called for all international airlines to stop flying to Russian airports. “Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such—not a single civilian aircraft,” he said. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account.” At the time, Ukraine did not have the means to act on Zelensky’s threat, one of the officials behind the operation told me. The military lacked the enormous fleet of specialized drones required to shut down Moscow’s airports for an extended period of time, he said. In response to Zelensky’s declaration, only one foreign carrier, Air Tanzania, briefly suspended flights to Moscow. Larger airlines, such as Emirates and Flydubai, continued as normal. “We didn’t follow through,” the Ukrainian official told me in frustration. Ukrainian arms manufacturers are still developing the specialized drone fleet, which relies on an AI-enabled technique known as map matching to identify targets and decide when to strike, the second person behind the plan told me. He said Ukraine first used this new type of drone in combat in mid-September, when a handful of them struck targets in the Russian-occupied region of Donetsk. They have not yet been deployed at scale against Russian airports, he added. [ Read: Inside the feud over Ukraine’s drone success ] Instead, the Ukrainian armed forces have used other weapons to achieve a similar effect. Rather than targeting airports directly, drones need only to appear in the sky around Moscow, forcing Russian authorities to cancel flights or close runways until the threat subsides. One adviser to Zelensky called it a “side effect” of Ukraine’s regular drone strikes against various targets in Russia. Zelensky prefers this approach because it does not involve targeting civilian aircraft. “That would be piracy,” the adviser, who has not been involved in the operation known as M&Ms, said. “The president doesn’t want to allow that.” His approach has still been disruptive for travelers in Russia. According to the tally from Echo of Moscow , the city’s airports restricted flights, on average, for more than three hours a day during the first full week of this month. On Friday, when Putin’s plane could not find a place to safely land in the capital, at least two of Moscow’s four airports remained closed to all flights for roughly seven hours. For regular citizens, these disruptions have been compounded by the new wave of Ukrainian strikes against Russian data centers. Most of the attacks have targeted the facilities of Yandex, a local counterpart to Google that acts as the backbone of Russia’s digital economy. Millions of Russians use its services every day, and many of them posted angry rants on social media in response to the latest outages. Yandex could need up to six months to repair the damage to its data centers, the Russian business newspaper Kommersant reported . As a bonus for Ukraine and many of its allies, the attacks appear to have caused a sharp decline in the activity of Russian bots across the internet, Zelensky noted in a video address to the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social-media platforms,” he said. “There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations, because there were fewer bots.” I n response to such attacks , the Russian military has expanded its strikes against civilians. Locomotives have become a favorite target. In August, 37 of them came under attack, more than one a day, the head of Ukraine’s state railway company, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, told me. Last month, the number rose to 47, including freight and passenger trains. When we met in Kyiv a few weeks ago, Pertsovskyi pulled out his phone and scrolled through a series of photos, each one showing trains torn apart by explosions. One of the gutted sleeper carriages had spilled its blackened cots and luggage onto the tracks. “This is how my mornings start now, with these reports and images, every day,” he said. A few days later, Russian drones prompted the evacuation of a train full of foreign dignitaries traveling from Kyiv to Poland, including David Petraeus, the former director of the CIA. One of the passengers, an American philanthropist, told me she walked through marshy fields in the middle of the night to get away from the train during an evacuation.The attack served as a reminder that no matter how creative Ukraine gets in targeting Moscow’s economic pressure points, Russia can always escalate, stomping on whatever norms remain untrampled in this war. Trump’s deal to buy Russian fuel will make that easier by inviting the Kremlin to top up its war chest with billions of dollars in export revenue. The deal also lifts some of the sanctions that the U.S. had imposed to punish and isolate Russia, leaving Putin with even less reason to accept a cease-fire. [ Read: Why would Europeans believe Trump now? ] For some members of Zelensky’s team, that act of American betrayal felt less like a setback for their strategy to win the war than it did the end of their best hope for victory. Even one of the officials behind the plan to shut down Moscow’s airports told me that if the U.S. sides with Russia, Ukraine would have little choice but to abandon the ladder of escalation and sue for peace. “There’s a realization now that Russia will not collapse because of its difficult economic situation,” he said. In offering a lifeline to Russia’s energy industry, Trump made the U.S. an obstacle to the Ukrainian strategy of wearing down the Russian economy and exhausting its population. “That means we need to change our strategy,” the official said. “Russia will not collapse, at least not now.” Ukraine still has plenty of ways to make life miserable in Russia, but it will likely take more than that to force Putin to accept a truce.

items.title: The Other AI Jobs
items.description: Want to get a job in the Bay Area? The fastest-growing listings are for operations engineers, applied scientists, senior machine-learning engineers, principal cloud architects, forward-deployed engineers, and the like, according to Laura Ullrich, the director of economic research in North America at the Indeed Hiring Lab. “A year ago, people were very concerned about these types of jobs not coming to fruition,” she told me. Today, “it’s all AI. It’s all AI jobs.” Or not quite all . Demand for estheticians, Pilates instructors, massage therapists, therapist therapists, and interior designers is also surging. And in a way, those are AI jobs too. It makes sense that someone earning seven figures a year at Anthropic would want a skilled person to untie the knots in their back and another to untie the knots in their psyche. Or that someone working a 72-hour-a-week, “ 996 ” schedule at Nvidia would not have time to shop for lamps for their Mission-style mansion on their own. Extraordinary wealth wants extraordinary luxuries. If history is any guide, what is happening in San Francisco and Santa Clara will happen in Indianapolis, Baton Rouge, and elsewhere too. AI will destroy jobs. AI will create jobs. And AI will create wealth that will create jobs—an obscure and overlooked aspect of how technological change shapes the labor market, and one that, in the long term, might be the most transformative. [ Annie Lowrey: Time to consider becoming a bricklayer ] AI and other general-purpose technologies—powerful and adaptable inventions, such as the printing press and the internet, rather than narrowly applicable (if cool!) innovations like the walkie-talkie and the IV—have first-order, second-order, and third-order effects on employment. ChatGPT and Claude Code, for example, are eradicating jobs for interpreters and call-center employees, and generating jobs for electricians constructing data centers and machine-learning experts constructing algorithms. That’s the first-order effect: direct, immediate, obvious. Then, AI is creating second-order roles for people applying, supporting, or iterating on the technology. These jobs are often “impossible” to imagine in advance, María Jesús Ramírez, a fellow at the McKinsey Global Institute, told me. To explain, she pointed to the development of the combustion engine in the late 1800s. The machine gave birth to the automobile industry and fueled the railroad boom. Eventually, “it creates aircraft,” she told me, “and now we have pilots.” But who would have looked at a furnace and anticipated the need for cabin stewards and air traffic controllers? More to the point, who would have played around with Gemini a year or two ago and predicted that companies would start hiring robot trainers , deepfake investigators , AI-risk underwriters, and AI-powered perfumers ? In a new report , Ramírez and her colleagues forecast that AI could create 500,000 to 2 million such novel positions in the coming years. But then there are the third-order jobs—let’s call them “wealth jobs”—that technologies create, which are even harder to fathom. Advances such as hydraulic pumps, GPS systems, and Wi-Fi tend to create a small coterie of capitalists with a fortune to spend on indulgences. They also allow businesses to do more with less, lowering prices, bumping up profits, increasing the number of goods and services on offer, and amplifying worker wages. This means the elite aren’t the only ones who get to indulge: Middle-class consumers have more money in their pockets and get a bigger bang for their buck at the store. “We become richer, and we can spend money on things or have jobs that, to our ancestors, would have been ridiculous,” explained Martha Gimbel, the executive director of the Yale Budget Lab. These jobs tend to be “things where you call your parents and you say, ‘I just paid someone to do X, and they say, ‘Martha, that is such a waste of money.’ Then they pause and go, ‘Was it great?’ And you’re like, ‘It was great, actually.’” Take wedding planners. “You could have done that job 200 years ago,” she said. “But who would have paid you to do it?” Nobody, more or less. Yet today, perhaps one in 10 American couples hires someone to handle the logistics on their big day. Or CrossFit trainers. “If you said to our ancestors, ‘People are going to pay huge amounts of money to throw tires across a room,’ they would have thought you were crazy,” Gimbel told me. She paused. “To be sure, people doing CrossFit are crazy.” Nevertheless, hundreds of thousands of them exist, forking over $200 a month to get fit. She noted that “water sommelier” is an actual position held by actual people, albeit just a few of them. [ Rogé Karma: Three ways to think about AI and jobs ] Wealth jobs tend to be service jobs: As incomes rise, families spend a higher portion of their paychecks on labor-intensive expenses such as higher education, health care, restaurant meals, and vacations, and a smaller portion on tradable goods, such as televisions and automobiles. Experts anticipate that AI will generate demand for in-person, face-to-face, personalized services in particular—the kind of things that LLMs and robots cannot and will never do. “People don’t want 10 cars,” Tanguy Catlin, also of the McKinsey Global Institute, told me. “They’re going to want to have something different, and I suspect there will be an emotional component to that.” Ullrich pointed to “wellness” services, meaning more jobs for cold-plunge installers, sauna technicians, and massage therapists. She also mentioned an uptick in hiring for house managers, people who will do your laundry and shopping and returns and keep your car registration up-to-date for you. (Swoon.) Still, the wealth jobs of the future will exist only if AI really generates wealth. If the technology proves too expensive for businesses to use, the average American’s wages won’t go up and they won’t have the cash to hire a therapist to talk them through a mushroom trip. And if the wealth AI produces never trickles down to middle-income Americans—perhaps because AI hollows out white-collar employment—it won’t generate many jobs either. Pretty much everyone I know would love to hire a house manager. Pretty much nobody I know can afford to hire one, yet.

items.title: Invasion of the Self-Replicating AI-Malware Botnet
items.description: Have you ever counted the computers in your house? Tally them up now. I’ll wait. You’re probably including your desktop and laptop computers, if you own some. I bet you’re also including the smartphones and tablets. Depending on the size of your family, that might mean 10 at most. Right? Your count is almost certainly wrong. I’ve got no fewer than 170 computers in my house. That’s because my home, like nearly everyone’s, is now chock-full of devices that a reasonable person might not even know are computers. Mine include speakers and thermostats, wall switches and electric plugs, door locks and cameras, printers and televisions, ceiling fans and window blinds. Robot vacuums, lawnmowers, and pool cleaners also log on. So do some refrigerators, toasters, and washing machines. And that’s just a sample. Together, this family of supposedly smart gadgets is sometimes referred to as the “internet of things,” or IoT. If you’ve got a thing that you interact with via an app, then it’s almost certainly online and chattering in the background. IoT gadgets have always been insecure, both by design (to simplify operation or allow them to phone home to a manufacturer) and by habit (because normal people are not network administrators who can secure them). If compromised by network exploits, default-password intrusion, or other security vulnerabilities, these devices—these computers—can be harnessed by malicious parties from anywhere in the world to overwhelm a target with a distributed denial-of-service attack; to relay traffic for fraud or hacking; to collect data for sale, use, or ransom; or to spread malware that perform these and other malicious acts. Homes aren’t the only targets, either. Businesses are also at risk, because so many of their operations involve machinery that has been (foolishly, but understandably) connected to the internet. Just this week, hackers attacked hundreds of French supermarkets , spoiling millions of dollars worth of food by warming up refrigerators and freezers remotely. None of this is new. But Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, published a blog post on Monday warning that artificial intelligence could make internet-of-things vulnerabilities worse. Ordinary malware follows the instructions its perpetrators wrote. That means it’s usually designed to exploit a specific vulnerability in a particular device—baby monitors, say—and then to use that vulnerability to run malicious software that does something specific, such as sending unwelcome traffic in a DDoS attack. AI introduces a new risk. Malware could install an AI model on many other nearby devices. Then a hostile program could, in effect, “chat” with that AI to carry out new kinds of pernicious acts. An Anthropic experiment successfully installed a small AI model across 15 Android TV boxes—the type of device that nearly every home contains, and that sends data to and from the internet constantly, even when the set appears to be turned off. Once the AI model is in place, malware programs with access could use it to help the malicious software gain access to even more devices, something that ordinary IoT exploits cannot do. That could help malware spread faster and more effectively. [ Peter Wehner: What if AI is the end of the world? ] The idea of a self-replicating AI botnet sounds profoundly dire, especially given the versions of that idea that philosophy and science fiction have imagined: Agent Smith copying himself over other people in The Matrix , the evolutionary swarm of autonomous machines in Stanisław Lew’s The Invincible , Nick Bostrom’s imagined machine so hell-bent on making paper clips that it extinguishes human life along the way. Recent worries about a hypothetically imminent AI-caused apocalypse have surely perked the public’s ear for anxiety about any type of wild AI fecundity. Not just We’re all gonna die , but A swarm of toasters and vacuum cleaners will be the agent of our doom . But AI-faciliated IoT malware is concerning for the opposite reason: because it is so ordinary and mundane. The millions of small, internet-connected computers that malicious actors might exploit have remained at least somewhat resilient because those attackers usually need to target them explicitly. External changes, such as firmware updates and network alterations, can limit or eliminate the threats. If malware has access to the rough equivalent of a tiny ChatGPT, however, it might be able to make previously difficult or uneconomical attacks newly possible. In the blog post, Anthropic notes that newer devices with built-in AI chips, such as video-conferencing units and security cameras, might become particularly attractive targets, because their hardware makes running a hostile AI model easier. Beyond those obvious marks, previously hard-to-target, low-value computers—including budget televisions, digital picture frames, smart appliances, or older devices left unused but still connected to a network—might become newly penetrable. The consequences of AI-accelerated malware remain more or less the same as those of the ordinary malware that is very likely running on your home network right now, without your knowledge. Instead of stealing your intimate photos or siphoning off your bank account, it mostly sends traffic to other networks, phones home with data to aggregate and sell, or routes traffic for shady activities to evade detection. That risk could expand should the AI-assisted spread that Anthropic predicts come to pass—a larger number of infected devices issuing greater disruption and facilitating more criminal activity and targeted exploitation. The self-replicating AI botnet does not issue a substantially new kind of threat—at least for now. But sometimes a quantitative increase in a risk’s exposure can produce a qualitative change in that risk’s consequence. Take antibiotic resistance, for example, or wildfires. When a landscape accrues substantially greater dried materials that can fuel a fire, the same number of successful ignitions can spread much faster and more broadly. Climate change, human expansion into wildlands, and invasive-species infestations, among other factors, have increased both the chances for fire and its consequences. Exposure to wildfire risk becomes much greater than the simple presence of additional kindling might suggest. An AI-assisted IoT malicious-software inundation could increase the impact of malware substantially. [ Matteo Wong: How long until AI hacks everything? ] Even then, the outcome would be more witless and banal than the wildfire metaphor suggests. AI-assisted software hacks could, in theory, mess with the actual computers on a network, as in the French-supermarket attack. But instead of shutting off your home’s smart fridge, coordinated, global, AI-enabled malware is more likely to make networked-computing life harder and more miserable for everyone. Email spam might offer a better metaphor for AI malware’s likely future. Junk email was annoying for years, but it remained manageable for a long time: You deleted the forwards from your weird uncle, and a simple spam filter caught much of the obvious junk. Eventually, though, email automation became cheap enough that it could both target enormous lists of addresses and personalize attacks, for phishing or exploitation. The low success rates of any single spam or phishing email ceased to be a problem once enormous mountains of junk email could be sent cheaply and easily. Now your inbox is ruined. Every email you receive from a stranger feels useless because you have begun to assume that email is all scams and garbage. (Phone calls and text messages are starting to feel the same way.) AI malware could follow suit, adjusting probes for greater success, slowing down every computer and network by overwhelming it with garbage-processing and traffic, issuing a nuisance arms race of vulnerability-driven updates and patches, and perhaps even assembling a patchwork of previously valueless local-network data into quilts of persistent, individualized deception or harassment. A dumb risk with good odds, if low consequence, might prove to be more awful than a terrifying one that is highly unlikely.

items.title: Un nouveau jalon historique : un astronaute pakistanais dans la station spatiale chinoise en 2026 (Par ZHAO Zhijin)
items.description: L’année 2026 s’affirme comme une année de percées exceptionnelles pour l’aérospatiale chinoise, marquée par des avancées technologiques majeures et une coopération internationale spatiale sans précédent. Parmi ces progrès, l’arrivée prochaine d’un astronaute pakistanais dans la station spatiale Tiangong constitue un nouveau jalon historique pour la cause spatiale chinoise et illustre la volonté de la Chine d’ouvrir largement ses plateformes spatiales au monde. Lors du 77e Congrès international d’astronautique, Yang Liwei, premier astronaute chinois, a salué les performances « extrêmement excellentes » des deux candidats astronautes pakistanais en formation. Après l’achèvement imminent de la mission Shenzhou-23, la Chine accueillera pour la première fois un astronaute étranger dans sa station spatiale dans la seconde moitié de 2026. L’un des deux astronautes pakistanais sélectionnés embarquera très probablement à bord de Shenzhou-24 pour une mission spatiale. Conformément au plan de mission, l’astronaute pakistanais participera à un vol spatial de courte durée en tant qu’expert de charge utile, principalement pour mener à bien des projets de recherche scientifique pakistanais. Afin de collaborer efficacement avec les astronautes chinois et d’utiliser normalement les équipements et systèmes de la station spatiale marqués en chinois, les deux candidats pakistanais ont suivi, entre autres, une formation intensive en chinois pendant plusieurs mois durant leur préparation. Cette future mission inaugurera une nouvelle ère de coopération sino-pakistanaise dans l’espace. Cette coopération est le fruit d’un partenariat solide et structuré. En février 2025, la Chine et le Pakistan ont signé à Islamabad un accord sur la sélection, la formation des astronautes pakistanais et leur participation aux missions de la station spatiale chinoise. À l’issue d’un processus rigoureux de sélection en trois étapes, deux candidats exceptionnels, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali et Khurram Daud, ont été officiellement retenus en avril 2026, concluant la première sélection d’astronautes étrangers du programme spatial habité chinois. Comme l’a souligné Yang Liwei, la station spatiale chinoise est devenue une plateforme scientifique ouverte aux chercheurs du monde entier. Elle favorise la coopération approfondie dans la recherche spatiale, la formation d’astronautes, l’octroi d’opportunités de vol et la vulgarisation scientifique. L’accueil d’un astronaute pakistanais incarne parfaitement cette vision d’ouverture et de partage des acquis spatiaux chinois. Parallèlement à cette coopération internationale, 2026 voit une accumulation de percées technologiques majeures pour la Chine. Le pays a validé avec succès deux technologies de récupération de fusées réutilisables, lui permettant de maîtriser cette technologie clé. Cette avancée réduira considérablement les coûts de lancement de satellites et accélérera le déploiement spatial national. De plus, un ou une astronaute de l’équipage de Shenzhou-23 restera dans la station spatiale pour une mission d’un an, devenant le premier membre d’équipage chinois à réaliser un séjour aussi long en orbite. Avec la mission sino-pakistanaise à venir et ces multiples innovations technologiques, la Chine confirme sa position d’acteur majeur et responsable de l’exploration spatiale mondiale, promouvant une exploration pacifique, inclusive et bénéfique pour tous. Par ZHAO Zhijin Journaliste de CGTN Français

items.title: Maaz Sadaqat sets sights on 2027 World Cup after ODI snub
items.description: Maaz Sadaqat may have missed out on selection for Pakistan’s upcoming One-day International (ODI) tri-series featuring England and Sri Lanka, but the swashbuckling left-hander has his sights firmly set on next year’s World Cup. The 21-year-old made a strong impression on the international stage in the recently concluded three-match T20I series against Sri Lanka, scoring consecutive half-centuries in the first two matches to help Pakistan clinch the series. His performances were more than just individual milestones, signalling a shift towards a more aggressive batting approach in T20 cricket, with Maaz emerging as a key figure in the change. He scored 50 off 29 balls in the opening match, helping Pakistan recover from an underwhelming powerplay alongside captain Sahibzada Farhan. In the second T20I, Maaz took the attack to the Sri Lankan bowlers, smashing 96 off 51 balls, including seven sixes and six fours, to come close to a maiden international century. His impressive run, however, will have to wait for another opportunity to continue in Pakistan colours, with the batter left out of the ODI squad despite having featured in six matches in the format, including his debut, earlier this year. Maaz had made an immediate impact in only his second ODI against Bangladesh, scoring 75 and taking three wickets with his left-arm spin. However, he struggled to maintain that form in the subsequent home series against Australia in May-June, managing scores of eight, zero and 27 on difficult surfaces. The reasons behind his omission from the squad for the upcoming tri-series remain unclear. The break, however, offers him an opportunity to refine his game with the 2027 World Cup in mind. “I am targeting the ODI World Cup and I am preparing for it,” Maaz said in a video interview released by the Pakistan Cricket Board on Thursday. “I have a 15-20-day window coming up which I am going to dedicate to working on myself for the World Cup.” The youngster, who rose from tape-ball cricket in Peshawar to become a franchise T20 sensation, has continued to build his reputation on the domestic and international circuits. He also struck two centuries in the recently concluded Caribbean Premier League season. Maaz believes the key to his progress lies in strengthening his natural game rather than focusing excessively on his weaknesses. “[In training] I try to work as much as I can on my strengths and less on my weaknesses, because if the ball is out of my range, I’d still be able to push it for a single or two,” he said. “However, if it is in my range, then I can hit it for six with my eyes closed. “If you watch both my CPL and international knocks, I keep a positive intent from the very start. “And if the ball comes in my range then I don’t spare it. And when a ball is a bit here or there, I try to rotate the strike.” That clarity of approach also extends to his preferred batting position. Although Maaz has previously said he is open to batting anywhere in the order, he admits he is most comfortable opening the innings. “I feel the most comfortable playing as an opener,” he said. A place in Pakistan’s squad for the 2027 World Cup would put Maaz in contention for an opening slot alongside Saim Ayub, who is averaging nearly 47, and experienced campaigner Fakhar Zaman. Maaz, however, views the competition for places as a challenge rather than a setback. “Even if I am asked to bat lower in the order, I’ll try to bat so well that they [team management] are forced to push me higher,” he said.

items.title: Les crises humanitaires du 21e siècle : la situation en Palestine
items.description: Les Palestiniens, forcés d’abandonner leurs terres, vivent sous occupation israélienne depuis plus de 55 ans. Au cours du 21e siècle, la situation s’est aggravée à la suite d’une succession d’évènement dramatique : le blocus de la bande de Gaza depuis 2007, la guerre à Gaza depuis octobre 2023 et une recrudescence des violences en Cisjordanie et à Jérusalem-Est. Depuis octobre 2023, Médecins du Monde (MDM) a alors œuvré pour une action humanitaire dans la région en ouvrant notamment des cliniques pour assurer des consultations de soins primaires. Aujourd’hui, l’enclavement de la bande de Gaza et les restrictions administratives de la part des autorités israéliennes en Cisjordanie interrogent sur la capacité d’action des ONG à pouvoir fournir une aide humanitaire convenable dans un contexte sous haute tension. Comment décririez-vous la situation humanitaire actuelle en Palestine ? Face à la volonté des autorités israéliennes d'interdire à 37 organisations non gouvernementales (ONG) internationales d'y opérer, comment Médecins du Monde (MDM) parvient-elle à préserver sa capacité d'action ? Comment les équipes humanitaires de MDM travaillent-elles sur le terrain alors que les bombardements israéliens ont réduit les infrastructures quasiment à néant ? Quelles sont les contraintes en matière d'accès aux civils et de protection des humanitaires ? Les violations répétées du droit international humanitaire, les attaques contre les soignants et les structures de santé, ainsi que les restrictions imposées aux ONG fragilisent-elles le principe même de l'action humanitaire et mettent-elles à mal l'ensemble du secteur de l'aide ? Le point avec Jean-François Corty, président de MDM et chercheur associé à l’IRIS L’article Les crises humanitaires du 21e siècle : la situation en Palestine est apparu en premier sur IRIS .
